title: Know your true cost before you set a price

say: Know your true cost before you set a price.
This is the video for Module 1 of Introduction to Pricing and Selling.
Every sale has three numbers behind it.
Cost is the money, and time, it takes you to make or buy the thing you sell.

panel.heading: Cost, price and profit
items: Cost: what it takes you to make or buy it
Price: what the customer pays you

say: Price is what the customer pays you.

panel.heading: Cost, price and profit
items: Cost: what it takes you to make or buy it
Price: what the customer pays you

say: Profit is what is left when you take cost away from price.
If a pack of chin chin costs you 550 naira to make and you sell it for 800 naira, your profit is 250 naira.

panel.heading: Cost, price and profit
items: Cost: what it takes you to make or buy it
Price: what the customer pays you

say: But if you sell it for 500 naira, you are losing 50 naira on every pack, even if your purse feels full.
Money coming in is called revenue. Revenue is not profit.

panel.heading: Cost, price and profit
items: Cost: what it takes you to make or buy it
Price: what the customer pays you

say: The first mistake is counting only materials.
Many sellers add up flour, sugar and oil, then stop. They forget packaging, transport, gas, phone data, and most of all, their own hours of work.

panel.heading: Three mistakes that keep sellers poor

say: The second mistake is copying the next seller's price.
She may buy in bulk, pay no rent, or be losing money without knowing it. Her price tells you about the market, not about your cost.

panel.heading: Three mistakes that keep sellers poor

say: The third mistake is never reviewing your price.
Flour, cooking gas and transport can change quickly. A price that gave a good profit six months ago can quietly turn into a loss.

panel.heading: Three mistakes that keep sellers poor

say: Here is the method. First, add your direct costs for one batch. These are the things that go into or onto the product, like ingredients, gas and packaging.
Use what you actually paid, from your receipts, not what you hope to pay.

panel.heading: Finding your true cost per item
items: Labour: your hours at a fair hourly rate
Divide by the number of good items

say: Second, add your labour. Ask what you could earn doing similar work for someone else.
If a day's work of 8 hours pays about 8,000 naira, your hour is worth about 1,000 naira.

panel.heading: Finding your true cost per item
items: Labour: your hours at a fair hourly rate
Divide by the number of good items

say: Third, add a share of overhead. That is stall rent, market levy, fuel, data, transport and POS charges. Add them for a month and share them across everything you make.

panel.heading: Finding your true cost per item
items: Labour: your hours at a fair hourly rate
Divide by the number of good items

say: Fourth, allow for waste. If 2 of every 40 packs are spoiled or tasted, divide by 38, not 40.

panel.heading: Finding your true cost per item
items: Labour: your hours at a fair hourly rate
Divide by the number of good items

say: Finally, divide the batch total by the number of good items.
The answer is your price floor. Below it, you lose money on every sale.

panel.heading: Finding your true cost per item
items: Labour: your hours at a fair hourly rate
Divide by the number of good items
panel.rule: Your true cost per item is your price floor.

say: Let us see this with Ngozi. She sells chin chin to offices and charges 500 naira a pack, because another seller does.
Her ingredients and gas cost about 13,000 naira, and packaging about 2,000 naira.
She works for 5 hours at 1,000 naira an hour, so 5,000 naira. Transport and data add 2,000 naira.
Her batch costs 22,000 naira. Divided by 40, that is 550 naira a pack.
At 500 naira she is giving away 50 naira of her labour on every sale. She is subsidising her customers.
Before you change any price, protect every payment. A common scam is the fake alert: a screenshot or SMS says money was sent, but nothing has entered your account.

panel.heading: What counts as proof of payment

say: Only trust money you can see in your balance inside your banking or wallet app. Check the amount and the sender name, then release the goods.
Never share your PIN, password or OTP, even with someone who says they are from your bank.

panel.heading: What counts as proof of payment

say: Set up these habits now. Keep business money in a separate account or wallet, and pay yourself a fixed wage on purpose.
Keep three records: a cost sheet, a price list and a daily sales book. And keep your receipts, so the real numbers are always there.

panel.heading: Three habits before you change prices
items: Separate business money from household money
Keep a cost sheet, price list and sales book
Keep receipts in one envelope or photo

say: To remember. Revenue is not profit. Count every cost, including your own time. A competitor's price shows the market, not your cost. Your true cost per item is your price floor. And confirm the money in your balance before you hand over any goods.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Revenue is money in; profit is what remains after costs
Count materials, packaging, overhead and your time
A competitor's price shows the market, not your cost
True cost per item is your price floor
Confirm money in your balance before releasing goods

say: Now choose one product you sell most often. Write its current price and how you chose it, then work out its true cost on a cost sheet.
Set up your record book with your own payment safety rule, and continue with the lessons below.

panel.heading: Your tasks for this module
items: Write your starting price and how you chose it
Complete a cost sheet for one product
Set up your record book and safety rule
